prompt: In TLS, SSH and WireGuard, which kind of cryptography encrypts the bytes of the conversation itself?
hint: What does each family do well?

choices.text: Asymmetric, because the data is what matters most
choices.why: Asymmetric runs for a few milliseconds at the start and carries no bulk data.

choices.text: Symmetric
choices.why: Right. The asymmetric half only agrees on the symmetric key.

choices.text: Both in turn, one packet each
choices.why: Nothing alternates: agreement once, then symmetric for every byte.

choices.text: Whichever the client proposes first
choices.why: The division of labour is fixed by what each half is good at.

prompt: A report says a 2048-bit RSA key is eight times stronger than a 256-bit AES key. What is wrong with the comparison?

choices.text: Nothing: more bits is more strength across families
choices.why: Bits mean different things in different families.

choices.text: RSA keys are measured in bytes, so it is sixty-four times
choices.why: Both are in bits; the families are what differ.

choices.text: Key lengths only compare within one family
choices.why: Right. RSA-2048 is roughly a 112-bit symmetric key.

choices.text: AES-256 is broken, so any RSA key wins
choices.why: AES with a 256-bit key is considered strong.

prompt: A colleague wants the payroll file encrypted with RSA instead of AES "because asymmetric is the stronger kind". What does the lesson answer?

choices.text: He is right; AES is kept for data nobody cares about
choices.why: AES carries every byte of TLS, SSH and WireGuard.

choices.text: Each family has its own job; bulk data is the symmetric one's
choices.why: Right. Asymmetric agrees on keys and signs.

choices.text: RSA would be fine if the key were 4096 bits
choices.why: Size is not the issue; RSA is the wrong tool for bulk data.

choices.text: Use both at once on every byte, for twice the strength
choices.why: Stacking ciphers is not the design any of these protocols uses.

prompt: seal.py encrypted a 30-byte instruction and printed how many bytes it sealed. How many of those bytes are the tag?
hint: Subtract the message from what was printed.

prompt: Somebody flips bits in payroll.enc, the AES-256-CBC file. What happens when it is decrypted with the right key?
hint: What does CBC say about changes?

choices.text: openssl reports that the file was altered
choices.why: CBC has no tag to check, so there is nothing to report with.

choices.text: The original message comes back, since the key is right
choices.why: The changed bits change the output.

choices.text: A different message comes out, and nothing says so
choices.why: Right. Secret, but not protected against change.

choices.text: Decryption refuses with InvalidTag
choices.why: That is AES-GCM, which CBC is not.

prompt: After one bit of the sealed message was flipped, what did box.decrypt return?
hint: Read the last line of the output.

choices.text: The message with one character changed
choices.why: That is how a bare cipher behaves.

choices.text: The message, plus a warning in the output
choices.why: Nothing of the message came back.

choices.text: Garbled bytes from the flipped block onwards
choices.why: GCM checks the tag before returning anything.

choices.text: Nothing: it raised InvalidTag
choices.why: Right. The message is refused whole.

prompt: GCM's one hard rule: two messages are never encrypted with the same key and the same ___.
In the X25519 exchange between laptop and app, what crossed the network?

choices.text: The two public keys
choices.why: Right. The private keys and the secret stayed where they were made.

choices.text: The shared secret, encrypted with app.pub
choices.why: The secret was computed on each side and never sent.

choices.text: ana.key, so that app could compute the same secret
choices.why: A private key that travels is no longer private.

choices.text: The sha256sum of the secret, to compare
choices.why: The hash was printed for the reader, not exchanged.

prompt: Both machines printed 72338c44…c5a2 after pkeyutl -derive. Which statements are true? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Each side combined its own private key with the other's public key
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The printed value is a hash of the secret, not the secret
choices.why: Right. That is why it was safe to show.

choices.text: Somebody who recorded both public keys could compute the same value
choices.why: Without a private key the secret is out of reach.

choices.text: It proves that app.pub really came from app
choices.why: Agreement proves nothing about identity.

prompt: On the way to laptop, app.pub was replaced by another machine's public key. laptop derives a secret as before. What does it end up with?
hint: Whose private key matches the public key laptop used?

choices.text: An error, because the key does not belong to app
choices.why: Nothing in X25519 knows which machine a key belongs to.

choices.text: A secret shared with app, since app's private key is unchanged
choices.why: laptop used the other public key, so app computes something else.

choices.text: A secret shared with whoever holds the matching private key
choices.why: Right. Perfectly encrypted, to the wrong party: identity is lessons 11 and 12.

choices.text: No usable secret, because the two hashes no longer match
choices.why: Nobody compares hashes in a real protocol; the secret works fine with the impostor.

prompt: A server's long-term key is stolen a year after a session was recorded. The session used fresh key pairs, thrown away afterwards. What does the thief get from the recording?
hint: Which keys made the session's secret?

choices.text: The whole session, since the long-term key unlocks it
choices.why: That is the case forward secrecy removes.

choices.text: The first packet, which the long-term key signed
choices.why: Signing does not encrypt anything.

choices.text: Half the session: the direction the server sent
choices.why: Both directions used the discarded keys.

choices.text: Nothing of the content
choices.why: Right. That is forward secrecy, as in TLS 1.3 and WireGuard.

prompt: How many RSA-2048 signatures a second did openssl speed measure on laptop?
Match each operation to how often a connection runs it.

pairs.right: on every byte of the connection
once, by the server, to prove its identity

right_distractors: once per packet, to check the tag

prompt: You run openssl speed on a small ARM board and every number is lower than laptop's. What should still hold?

choices.text: The 3,313 signatures a second, since RSA-2048 is a fixed amount of work
choices.why: The absolute numbers belong to one machine on one afternoon.

choices.text: Symmetric far ahead of the key agreement and the signature
choices.why: Right. The ratios are what travel.

choices.text: X25519 beats AES-GCM there, lacking the AES instructions
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson supports the order flipping.

choices.text: None of it; each machine is a new design question
choices.why: The design rests on ratios that hold across machines.

prompt: In wire.txt, how many bytes did the two handshake packets carry together?
A packet arrives at fw through wg0 from the branch's peer with source address 192.168.40.5. What happens to it?

choices.text: It is forwarded, since it came through the encrypted tunnel
choices.why: The tunnel checks the source too.

choices.text: Dropped: that source is outside AllowedIPs
choices.why: Right. AllowedIPs is a filter as well as a route.

choices.text: It is answered with a new handshake
choices.why: A handshake does not widen what a peer may send.

choices.text: It is routed back to the internet segment through eth0
choices.why: It never gets that far.

prompt: What does somebody recording the internet segment between the two routers learn?

choices.text: The URL the branch asked for
choices.why: The request travelled inside ChaCha20-Poly1305.

choices.text: Nothing at all
choices.why: The addresses, the port, the times and the sizes are in the clear.

choices.text: The session key, from the 148-byte packet
choices.why: The handshake agrees the key without sending it.

choices.text: That the offices talk, when, and how much
choices.why: Right. Not what was said.

prompt: From a branch computer, somebody tries SSH on port 22 of 192.168.20.10 through the tunnel. What decides the outcome, and what is it?
hint: What does a packet leaving wg0 still cross?

choices.text: WireGuard: the peer is trusted, so it connects
choices.why: A VPN decides who joins, not what they reach.

choices.text: AllowedIPs, which lists ports; 22 is absent
choices.why: AllowedIPs lists addresses, not ports.

choices.text: fw's forward chain, whose rule allows the branch only 8080
choices.why: Right. The matrix of lesson 4 still applies.

choices.text: The handshake, which refuses non-HTTP traffic
choices.why: The handshake knows nothing of what will be carried.

prompt: Order what happens between fw and branch, from first to last.
items: each router makes a Curve25519 key pair
each configuration names the other side's public key
the handshake turns the key pairs into fresh symmetric keys
ChaCha20-Poly1305 carries the request and its answer
trap: A handshake needs the peer's public key already in the configuration.

prompt: Match each requirement to the mechanism in this lesson that meets it.

pairs.left: a changed bit must be refused
two ends that never met need a common key
a key stolen next year must not open today's recording
the tunnel accepts only the branch's addresses

prompt: A team plans to encrypt 40 GB of nightly backups for a remote site by running every block through RSA with the site's public key. What design does this lesson point to instead?
hint: Which operation is fast, and which runs once?

choices.text: Keep RSA, with 4096-bit keys for backups
choices.why: A larger key makes each operation slower still.

choices.text: A symmetric AEAD for the data, with the asymmetric half used once for its key
choices.why: Right. Slow once, fast for every byte.

choices.text: AES-CBC with a password, run through 600,000 PBKDF2 rounds
choices.why: Fast, but a changed backup would decrypt without complaint.

choices.text: X25519 on every block instead of RSA
choices.why: X25519 agrees keys; it does not encrypt data.

prompt: An internal tool stores payment instructions encrypted with AES-256-CBC. Nobody else has the key. What should an audit report about it?
hint: Secret is one property. What is the other?

choices.text: An altered instruction would decrypt without error; use AES-GCM
choices.why: Right. Authenticated encryption refuses it.

choices.text: Nothing, since only the tool holds the key
choices.why: Keeping the key secret does not detect a change.

choices.text: AES-256 is too weak; move the instructions to RSA-2048
choices.why: RSA-2048 is about 112-bit strength, below AES-256.

choices.text: Raise -iter above 600,000
choices.why: Iterations harden a typed password, not the message.
